EVIDENCE & ASSUMPTIONS

Real questions.
Transparent assumptions.

The 75% / 56% finding

The earlier 75% / 56% comparison could not be reproduced from a documented method. We inspected all 181,929 rows of the Foundations dataset; its fields do not directly distinguish extra rooms from new rooftop homes. Keyword results change substantially when procedural applications are excluded. No substitute percentages are presented as validated rates.

Any comparison needs explicit text filters, decision categories, sample sizes and an audit of how applications are classified. Group approval rates would not predict this roof’s outcome or prove that creating a home causes refusal.

The simulator

The coordinates, council boundaries and mapped footprints are real. The proposal, dwelling layout, financial assumptions and actor-support scores are illustrative. Presets are station/neighbourhood anchors, not vacant sites or housing allocations. The overlay implies no right to develop.

What the scores mean

Scores run from 0 to 100. More storeys increase design capacity and viability but reduce neighbour support. Setbacks improve amenity and policy fit but reduce usable space. Screening helps privacy and adds cost. An illustrative mitigation budget improves policy fit while reducing viability. No score is a probability.

“Compare a compromise” searches storeys, half-metre setbacks, screening, budget in £10k steps while holding your selected affordable target, maximising the lowest actor score. A 60-point threshold is a teaching choice, not planning policy. The new-block estimate assumes 80% usable area and 75 m² per home, with a 30 × 24 m initial footprint. Rooftop housing assumes two homes per floor. Neither is a space-standards assessment.

Exact score assumptions

F = storeys for roof schemes, or storeys ÷ 3 for blocks. S = setback in metres. C = mitigation budget in £1,000s, zero for rooms. A = affordable percentage ÷ 5, zero for rooms. P = 1 with screening, otherwise 0. H = max(0, proposed block height ÷ median mapped-context height − 1) × 8; zero for roof schemes. Scores are rounded and limited to 0–100.

  • Architect: 78 + 7F − 6S.
  • Developer: 64 + 10F − 8S − 0.16C − 1.5A − 4P.
  • Planning: 45 + (12 for homes; 5 for rooms) + 9S − 8F + 0.18C + 1.5A + 5P − 0.5H.
  • Residents: 70 − 15F + 11S + 12P − H.

Local context height affects the illustrative model. Council-specific documents are shown separately: they do not become invented council “strictness” scores. Median context height uses OSM height tags, storeys × 3 m where recorded, and an assumed 9 m otherwise. This is not a daylight, overlooking or heritage assessment. Roof schemes use that median as a notional base height, not a surveyed building height.

Geographic data

GLA borough boundaries locate the council using point-in-polygon matching. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0; GLA / Ordnance Survey Open Data. Geometry references 2017 geography, not a new survey.

Footprints and street geometry: © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. Three neighbourhood extracts are saved locally; custom sites load a small live extract. Complex multipolygon buildings may be incomplete. Heights may be estimated and flat roofs are simplified. TfL station coordinates provide the preset anchors.

Planning sources

Checked 26 September 2026. A roof extension within an existing home is treated differently from additional independent dwellings. Small schemes can still attract locally justified obligations; the model does not impose a universal tariff.

  • GOV.UK: planning obligations and the legal tests
  • Islington: obligations on additional homes, including small sites
  • GOV.UK: consultation and pre-decision matters
  • GOV.UK: determining an application
  • House London: source planning dataset

Affordability routes depend on current policy and eligibility. A time-limited 2026 London route means an unqualified “35% everywhere” assumption would be misleading.
